segments.original: When future generations look back on the first decade of the 21st century, they may see it as something of a golden age of European cinema. For it was during this period that European Union incentives, introduced in the 1990s, finally bore fruit: once the material advantages for directors and producers working within Europe had been proven, co-productions stopped being the exception and became the norm.

segments.original: Filmmakers such as Michael Haneke (b. 1942) and Paul Verhoeven (b. 1938) can move between different countries - including the United States - without losing their identities as auteurs. Antichrist (2009), by Lars von Trier (b. 1956), was made with European money but shot in English; its leads were a Frenchwoman and an American. However, between that film and Dogville (2003), Von Trier made De Fem Bespaend (The Five Obstructions, 2003) and Direktøren for Det Hele (The Boss of It All, 2006), the two films in his body of work most concerned with Danish issues.

segments.original: Von Trier is perhaps the greatest example of this malleable form of nationalism and auteur identity. Although he had already made an English-language film in 1996 - Breaking the Waves (1996) - the year 2000 marked the release of his first truly international production, Dancer in the Dark (2000). Starring Björk, the film won two awards at that year's Cannes Film Festival - among them the Palme d'Or. The Swedish film Män Som Hatar Kvinnor (The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, 2009), adapted by Niels Arden Oplev (b. 1961) from the novel by fellow Scandinavian Stieg Larsson, proved a hit with both critics and audiences, and an American adaptation was soon planned for 2011.

segments.original: The two countries that had struggled to find a coherent cinematic identity during the 1980s and 1990s - Germany and Italy - gave rise to two quite distinct, even divergent, movements in the 2000s. From Germany came a series of big-budget films that dealt with historical events without being nostalgic in any way, but were marked by a concern with the country's turbulent past. After directing the modern Das Experiment (The Experiment, 2001), a contemporary look at Nazi psychology, Oliver Hirschbiegel (b. 1957) made, in 2004, Der Untergang (Downfall, 2004), which chronicled the dictator's final days.

segments.original: Yet perhaps it was the Cold War surveillance drama Das Leben der Anderen (The Lives of Others, 2006), directed by Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck (b. 1973), that defined German cinema in the 2000s. The film achieved immense popularity around the world, even winning an Oscar, but it also stirred controversy for its deeply moving and sympathetic portrayal of an officer of the Stasi, the secret police of the German Democratic Republic.

segments.original: To the defenders of these films, they represented a belated reckoning by the German film industry with the Nazi past. Their detractors, on the other hand, dismissed them as cynical and insensitive attempts to profit from it. The Austrian-German Die Fälscher (The Counterfeiters, 2007), by Stefan Ruzowitzky (b. 1961), attracted considerable attention. Austrian cinema had long been seen as the poor cousin of German cinema, but in the 2000s it was on the rise. Young filmmakers (often women) who came out of the Vienna Film Academy, such as Jessica Hausner (b. 1972), with Lourdes (2009), and Valeska Grisebach (b. 1968), with Sehnsucht (Longing, 2006), produced subtle and original works that sparked international interest.

segments.original: Italy also looked to the past, but with very different results. Marco Bellocchio (b. 1939) created an unsettling dramatization of the terrorist activities of the 1970s in Buongiorno, notte (Good Morning, Night, 2003). This film, together with Le conseguenze dell'amore (The Consequences of Love, 2004), by Paolo Sorrentino (b. 1970), became a calling card for a new generation of Italian directors, who spoke out both verbally and cinematically against the unbearable weight of the filmic nostalgia that had either stifled the country's cinema or reduced it to a cheap imitation of itself over the previous two decades.

segments.original: Direct criticism of Silvio Berlusconi's contemporary government was almost impossible, thanks to deplorable acts of censorship. Nevertheless, films such as Mio fratello è figlio unico (My Brother Is an Only Child, 2007) and Gomorra (Gomorrah, 2008) delve into violence and corruption in Italy past and present. These directors' current perspective is marked by new aesthetic approaches that tend to be overstylized, or frenetic and flamboyant, though painted in dull, faded tones - an antidote, perhaps, to the sun-drenched melodramas of the 1980s and the languid pace of the 1960s and of directors such as Michelangelo Antonioni (1921-2007) and Federico Fellini (1920-1993).

segments.original: The United Kingdom, France, and Germany in particular witnessed the emergence of a large number of second- and third-generation directors from ethnic minorities, such as Gurinder Chadha (b. 1960) and Asif Kapadia (b. 1972), Abdellatif Kechiche (b. 1960) and Rachid Bouchareb (b. 1953), Fatih Akin (b. 1973) and Thomas Arslan (b. 1962). Their works deal with issues such as social integration and the way hybrid cultures are negotiated. In Germany, Akin, a Turkish-German filmmaker, set out to change the German perception of a monocultural, ethnically homogeneous society with films such as Gegen die Wand (Head-On, 2004). The Belgian brothers Jean-Pierre (b. 1951) and Luc Dardenne (b. 1954), winners of the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival, were perhaps a classic case of festival filmmakers, 21st-century poetic realists whose bleak reflections on life among the lowest strata of society were acclaimed by critics but failed to draw audiences.

segments.original: Within what came to be called the new Europe, however, Romania proved to be an exception. Elsewhere, the tendency was for the representation of national cinemas to be limited to a handful of filmmakers who seemed to burst suddenly onto the international circuit, only to fall back into obscurity. Examples include Bosnian Danis Tanovic (b. 1969), with No Man's Land (2001), and Hungarian György Pálfi (b. 1974), with Taxidermia (2006). The early 21st century marked a period of prosperity for European cinema, but the gulf between Eastern and Western Europe remains the same.
